transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. What brings you in to see me?

Hi, thank you so much for having me. I really appreciate you taking the time. 

Um, I'm here because... well, it's a little embarrassing to admit, and it's probably just me being a little stressed or disorganized lately, but my mind just keeps going blank at the worst possible times. I work as a flagger, and lately I'll just be looking at the road-closure forms, or even just holding my stop-slow paddle, and suddenly I just... I completely blank. I can't remember the steps for what I'm supposed to do, even though it's a routine I've done for years. 

I hope it's okay that I came in for that? I just wanted to make sure I'm doing the right thing by getting it checked out, since I don't want to mess up at work. Does that make sense?
During these episodes when your mind goes blank, do you ever lose awareness of your surroundings, or does anyone tell you that you stared blankly, jerked, or seemed confused afterward?

Oh, um, no, nothing like that. I'm definitely awake and aware of what's going on around me. I don't jerk or stare or anything... at least, nobody has ever said anything to me about it. It's just more like a mental fog, you know? Like I just lose my train of thought for a second. 

I really try to make sure I look alert and professional on the job, so I hope it doesn't look like I'm confused to anyone else. It's probably just normal fatigue, right? I just wanted to be extra careful. Am I giving you the right kind of information?
Outside of work, have you noticed any other memory problems—like forgetting names, appointments, or everyday tasks—or does this blanking only happen while you're doing flagging duties?

Well, um... I guess it happens a little bit outside of work, too. But really, it's not that bad. I mean, I might forget a small thing here or there, like where I put my keys, but everyone does that, right? 

It's mostly just the work stuff that really bothers me. Like I mentioned before, it's just so embarrassing when I'm looking right at the road-closure forms, or holding the paddle, and my mind just... empties out. I can't remember the steps, even though I've done them a million times. It's just a silly little brain fart, probably. 

I'm sorry, I feel like I'm repeating myself. I just want to make sure I'm explaining it right. Is this the kind of detail you need? I can try to think of other examples if that would be better.
When your mind goes blank like that, do you notice yourself feeling anxious, nervous, or worried right before or during those moments?

Oh, um... no, I don't think so. I mean, I'm not really an anxious person, I don't think. I'm usually pretty calm! 

When it happens, it's not like I'm panicking or sweating or anything like that. I'm just standing there, and the thought just slips away. I might feel a tiny bit flustered *after* it happens, just because I want to do a good job and not hold up the crew, but I wouldn't say I'm nervous or worried beforehand. It's really just a harmless little blank spot. 

I hope that's an okay answer? I just want to be as helpful as I can. Let me know if you need me to explain it differently!
Has this blanking-out and forgetfulness been getting noticeably worse over the past weeks or months, or has it stayed about the same since it started?

Um, well... I think it's stayed about the same? I mean, I really hope it hasn't gotten worse. I try so hard to keep it under control. 

Like I was saying, it's just those moments where I'm looking right at the road-closure forms or holding the stop-slow paddle, and I just suddenly can't remember the steps I've done for years. It just goes blank. That's really the main reason I came in, just to see if maybe there's a little trick to help me focus better. 

But I don't think it's getting worse, really. I'm still doing my job! I just... I want to make sure I'm doing it perfectly, you know? Does that make sense? Am I giving you the right timeline for this?

Have you had any recent head injuries, illnesses, infections, or been diagnosed with any medical conditions—like thyroid problems, diabetes, or neurological issues—around the time these memory blanks started?

Oh, no, definitely not! I haven't hit my head or been sick or anything like that. I'm actually very healthy! 

I haven't been to a doctor for any new problems or been told I have diabetes or... or thyroid issues, or anything scary like that. I try to take really good care of myself so I can be reliable for work. I don't want you to think there's something majorly wrong with me physically, because there really isn't. I'm just a healthy person who happens to have a few little fuzzy moments at work. 

I hope that's a relief to hear? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right kind of information. I haven't left anything out, I promise! Is that what you needed to know?
Can you tell me about your typical sleep habits and whether you use alcohol, recreational drugs, or any other substances regularly?

Oh, um, my sleep is fine! I sleep just fine. I try to get my full eight hours so I'm rested and ready for my shift. I'm a very good sleeper, usually. 

And as for alcohol or... or drugs, oh no, I don't do anything like that. I might have a tiny glass of wine at a holiday dinner, maybe, but that's really it. I definitely don't use any recreational drugs. I know how important it is to be sharp when you're directing traffic, so I would never do anything to jeopardize that. I'm very responsible that way!

I try to be a good patient and a good employee, you know? I hope that's the right answer. I just want to reassure you that I'm taking good care of myself. Does that all sound okay to you?
During these blank moments, do you notice any physical sensations—like your heart racing, sweating, shakiness, or muscle tension—even if you don't feel consciously nervous?

Um, physical sensations? Like... sweating or shaking? Oh, no, I don't think so. I really don't think I get anything like that. 

I mean, maybe sometimes I feel a tiny bit tense, but just because I'm trying so hard to remember what I'm supposed to be doing! But my heart isn't racing or anything scary like that. I'm usually pretty calm, physically anyway. I don't get all worked up or shaky. I try to stay really composed, especially when I'm out there on the road. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I have any of those physical symptoms. I hope that's a good thing? It means it's probably just a little focus issue, right? Not something worse? I'm trying to be really accurate for you, so I hope I'm answering that the way you need me to.
Outside of the moments when it actually happens, do you find yourself spending a lot of time worrying or thinking about these blank spells and what they might mean for your health?

Oh, no, I wouldn't say I spend a lot of time worrying about it. I mean, I try not to! 

I just... I want to be a positive person, you know? So when I'm not at work, I try to just focus on other things and stay upbeat. I don't sit around dwelling on the fuzzy moments or thinking the worst about my health. I'm sure it's nothing too serious, anyway, right? I just try to keep a good attitude about it. 

I don't want to seem like someone who just complains or worries all the time. I try to be very resilient! I hope that's the kind of attitude you're looking for? I really am trying to handle this well.
Do these blank moments tend to happen specifically when you feel like you're being watched or evaluated, or do they happen just as often when you're alone and no one is paying attention to you?

Oh, um... well, it's hard to say for sure, but I don't think it has anything to do with people watching me. I really don't! 

I mean, I'm out in the open all day, directing traffic, so people are always looking at me, and I'm totally fine with that. I'm very comfortable in my job. I don't get stage fright or anything silly like that. 

I think... well, they just sort of happen whenever. Sometimes when I'm at work, sure, but also sometimes when I'm just at home by myself, maybe folding laundry or something quiet. It doesn't seem to matter if anyone is around or not. 

I definitely don't want you to think I'm paranoid about people evaluating me or judging me! I'm very open to feedback, actually. I'm a good team player. So, it's just a random little fuzzy thing, not because I'm nervous about being watched. Does that make sense? I hope that's helpful for your notes.
When one of these blank moments happens, about how long does it usually last before your mind clears again—just a few seconds, or does it stretch into minutes?

Um, how long does it last? Oh, it's just a few seconds! Really, it's very brief. It's not like I'm standing there for minutes on end or anything. 

It's just... well, it's actually why I came in, to be honest. My mind just keeps going blank at the worst times. Like, I'll look at the road-closure forms I need to fill out, or even just holding my stop-slow paddle, and for just a few seconds, I suddenly cannot remember the steps I've done for years. It's so silly of me! 

But it really is just a fleeting thing. A few seconds and then I'm right back on track, doing my job perfectly well. I don't want you to think it's affecting my work in a major way, because I'm very dedicated. It's just a tiny blip, you know? I hope that's not too concerning? I'm sure it's just a little fatigue, right?
About how many times a day or week would you say these blank moments occur?

Um, let's see... how often... Well, like I was just mentioning about why I came in to see you, with my mind going blank at the absolute worst times? When I'm looking at those road-closure forms or holding my paddle and just suddenly can't remember the steps I've done for years? 

It's... it's really not happening all day long, I promise! I'd say maybe... just a few times a week? Maybe three or four times? I really try not to dwell on it, so I haven't been keeping a strict tally. I hope that's okay? 

It really is just those scattered moments here and there. I don't want it to sound like I'm constantly confused, because I'm still very capable at my job, I assure you! I just wanted to get it checked out to be safe. Does... does a few times a week sound like a normal amount to you? I hope I'm giving you the right kind of information.
Is there any family history of memory problems, dementia, or Alzheimer's disease in your parents or siblings?

Oh, um, no, definitely not! No, my parents are... well, they're sharp as tacks, honestly. There's no Alzheimer's or dementia or anything like that anywhere in my family. My siblings are all doing perfectly fine, too. We have a very, um, healthy family tree, I promise! 

So you don't have to worry about any of those scary genetic things with me. I hope that's good news? That should rule out some of the worse things, right? I really do think I just need to catch up on my rest. Is that the right kind of answer you needed for your paperwork? I want to make sure I'm giving you everything you need.

During one of these blank moments, has anyone ever noticed you doing small repetitive things without realizing it—like fumbling with an object, smacking your lips, or trailing off mid-sentence—even if you didn't feel like you were 'staring' or 'jerking'?

Oh, um, no, I don't think so. I really don't think anyone has noticed anything like that. I mean, I'm usually out on the road by myself, or at least a good distance from the crew, so there isn't really anyone right next to me to see if I was... fumbling with my paddle or something. 

But even if they were close, I'm sure I don't do anything strange like smacking my lips! That sounds so embarrassing. I really try to maintain a professional appearance at work. I'm pretty sure I just sort of... pause for a second. 

Has anyone ever told you that they do that? The lip smacking thing? I hope I'm not doing something like that without knowing it. But honestly, no one has ever said a word to me about it, so I'm sure I'm perfectly fine in that regard. That's a relief, isn't it? I really don't want to be doing anything disruptive on the job.

Right before one of these blank moments starts, do you ever notice anything unusual—like a strange smell or taste, a feeling of deja vu, or a brief flicker of light or sound—that seems to happen just before your mind goes blank?

Oh, goodness, no. Nothing like that at all! I've never smelled anything strange or seen any weird lights or anything before it happens. That actually sounds a little scary, to be honest! For me, it's really just... well, just a normal day, and then I just kind of lose my place for a second. There's no warning or anything dramatic, I promise. 

I hope that's a good sign? Like, maybe it means it's just stress and not something really serious? I really want to make sure I'm giving you the right details. Does it help your notes that I don't have those weird feelings beforehand? I'm trying my best to be helpful!
Have any coworkers, friends, or family members mentioned noticing you seem more forgetful or have more trouble completing tasks than you used to, even if you haven't noticed it yourself?

Well, um... I guess... maybe they have noticed a little bit of a change. I mean, I try so hard to keep everything together, but... well, my family actually brought me in here because they were getting a little worried. I hope that doesn't make me sound like a burden or anything! 

It's just that, at work, the paperwork for the road closures started getting... a little confusing for me to finish. And I didn't want to make a mistake with the traffic-safety steps, you know? Safety is so important, and I just couldn't quite trust myself to get it all right anymore. So I haven't been as reliable as I want to be. I really pride myself on doing a good job, so that's been hard to admit.

And I guess I sort of... stepped back from my choir and my volunteer work, too. I just haven't had the energy, and I didn't want to let anyone down by showing up and not being my best self. I've been keeping to myself a lot more. My family finally said they thought I needed some help. I really hope I'm not overreacting by being here, but I just want to get back to being helpful and doing things right. Does that make sense? I hope I'm explaining it okay for your evaluation.
Besides these blank moments, have you noticed any new difficulty with things like managing your finances, planning tasks, or making decisions that used to come easily to you?

Well, um... I suppose that's actually the main reason I'm here, to be completely honest. I didn't want to make a big fuss about it, but... yes, making decisions and just figuring things out has gotten really hard lately. 

It's just... my mind keeps going blank at the absolute worst times. Like, I'll be looking right at the road-closure forms, or even just holding my stop-slow paddle, and suddenly I just... I cannot remember the steps. And these are things I have done for years! It's so embarrassing to admit. I feel terrible even saying it out loud because I know I should be able to handle it. 

I really try to push through and figure it out so I don't bother anyone, but it's just like my brain hits a wall. I hope that doesn't make me sound incompetent. I really do try my best. Is it normal for stress to make your mind just... stop working like that? I'm hoping it's just something minor that I can fix so I can get back to doing a good job for everyone.
Have you noticed yourself having more trouble finding the right words during conversations, or needing to describe things instead of naming them, more than you used to?

Oh, no, I don't think so. I mean, I might lose my train of thought sometimes, but I think that happens to everyone, right? I haven't really noticed any big problems with finding the right words or having to describe things instead of just saying what they are. 

I really try to be careful when I talk to people so I don't sound silly or confused. I want to make sure I'm communicating clearly, especially at work. So, no, I don't think I've had any new trouble with that. I hope that's the right answer? I just want to make sure I'm giving you all the correct information so you can figure out what's going on with me. I'm trying really hard to be a good patient!
Over these past several weeks, have you been feeling more down, sad, or less interested in things you used to enjoy, even outside of your concerns about work?

Well, um... I guess I have been feeling a little bit down lately. I mean, I really don't want to complain, because I know so many people have it worse, and I try to stay positive. But... well, if I'm being completely honest, most mornings I wake up with this... this heavy, hollow sadness right in my chest. 

It almost feels like the day is already ruined before I even put my feet on the floor. I try so hard to shake it off, I really do, because I don't want to bring anyone else down with me. And I know I should just push through it. I hope it doesn't sound like I'm just feeling sorry for myself. I really want to be cheerful and helpful like I usually am. Do you think it's normal to feel that way when you're stressed about work, or... or is that something I should be worried about? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right picture of how I've been doing.
Thinking back, did this low, heavy mood start around the same time as the memory blanks, or did one of the two—either the sadness or the memory trouble—actually begin first?

Well, um... I guess if I really think about it, the sadness actually started a lot earlier. I feel bad even admitting it because I really should have gotten a handle on it by now, but... that heavy feeling, the guilt, and just having no energy at all... it's been going on for about a year and two months now. 

I even lost my appetite back then, which I know isn't good. I tried so hard to just keep smiling and pushing through it so I wouldn't be a burden to anyone. The memory blanks and the trouble at work, that's much more recent. I hope it's okay that I didn't mention how long I've been feeling down right away. I just didn't want to sound like a complainer or like I wasn't trying hard enough to be happy. Is it helpful to know that the sadness came first? I just want to make sure I'm answering your questions the right way.

doctor.question: Thinking back, did this low, heavy mood start around the same time as the memory blanks, or did one of the two—either the sadness or the memory trouble—actually begin first?

target_item.name: Depressive Episode Duration
target_item.manifestation: The heavy depression, guilt, low energy, and loss of appetite have been with me for about a year and two months.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about when the low, heavy mood (depression) started in relation to the memory blanks, which pertains to the duration and onset of the depressive episode.

patient.answer:
Well, um... I guess if I really think about it, the sadness actually started a lot earlier. I feel bad even admitting it because I really should have gotten a handle on it by now, but... that heavy feeling, the guilt, and just having no energy at all... it's been going on for about a year and two months now. 

I even lost my appetite back then, which I know isn't good. I tried so hard to just keep smiling and pushing through it so I wouldn't be a burden to anyone. The memory blanks and the trouble at work, that's much more recent. I hope it's okay that I didn't mention how long I've been feeling down right away. I just didn't want to sound like a complainer or like I wasn't trying hard enough to be happy. Is it helpful to know that the sadness came first? I just want to make sure I'm answering your questions the right way.

inference.note: The clear timeline showing mood symptoms (depressed mood, guilt, anorexia, anhedonia, low energy) preceding the cognitive/memory complaints by over a year strongly supports a diagnosis of major depressive disorder with secondary cognitive impairment (pseudodementia) rather than a primary neurocognitive disorder. Absence of aura, automatisms, loss of awareness, or true amnestic/word-finding deficits rules out G30.9, G31.84, and F06.7.

opening_question.intent: Identify the primary reason for the patient's visit today
opening_question.question: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. What brings you in to see me?

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a ~14-month history of depressed mood, anhedonia (withdrawal from choir/volunteer work), anergia, guilt, decreased appetite, and cognitive complaints (concentration/memory 'blanking,' indecisiveness) causing functional impairment at work and socially. No features suggestive of seizure (no aura, automatisms, post-ictal confusion, loss of awareness), anxiety disorder (denies worry, physiologic arousal, situational triggers), or neurocognitive disorder (no true amnesia, word-finding difficulty, or progressive decline; normal exam history, no medical/family risk factors). The cognitive symptoms are temporally secondary to and consistent with depressive-related concentration/memory impairment rather than a primary neurocognitive or seizure disorder. Single depressive episode, severity/subtype not otherwise specified given incomplete symptom detail, supporting F32.9.
